findings.title: Google credential is overwritten with a safeParse result object
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the zod `safeParse` result (`{ success, data }`, see `parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:29`). It does not return the parsed data. Line 97 assigns that object to `key`, and line 100 writes `data: { key }`. The old code used `googleCredentialSchema.parse(...)`, which returned the credential itself. After the first token refresh, the stored Google credential is `{ success: true, data: {...} }`. The next `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in the constructor (line 75) then fails, so every Google Calendar connection breaks once its token expires. Use `.data` here: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data`.

findings.title: Computed keys in minimumTokenResponseSchema are "[object Object]", so sync mode always throws
findings.body:
`[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to the literal string `"[object Object]"`. So the schema requires a numeric property named `"[object Object]"`. Line 10 adds an optional property under the same key, which collides with it. No real token response has that property, so with credential sharing enabled every `parseRefreshTokenResponse` call throws "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Zod object schemas cannot express "any number-valued key" this way. Use `z.object({ access_token: z.string() }).passthrough()`. If an expiry field is required, name it explicitly or check it by hand.

Separately, lines 25-27 write the placeholder `"refresh_token"` into the response whenever `refresh_token` is missing. Callers persist that value, so a fake refresh token can end up stored in the credential. In sync mode, a later switch back to direct refresh would then send it to the provider. Keep the placeholder out of anything that gets stored.

findings.title: Return type is a SafeParse result but callers treat it inconsistently
findings.body: The helper returns a `SafeParseReturnType` after throwing on failure, so `success` is always true. Callers then disagree on what they have: Google stores it whole (see the blocker finding). Office365 (`office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:264`) and Zoom/Salesforce still check `.success`/`.data`, which is dead code. Return `refreshTokenResponse.data` and update the callers. Also, Office365 previously tolerated a failed parse by logging and continuing with the old credentials. It now throws, which changes behaviour for non-sync users with no mention in the PR.

findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in the Salesforce service
findings.body: Line 96 calls `prisma.credential.update`, but the file has no `prisma` import (the only match for `prisma` in the file is this line). This fails type checking and throws a ReferenceError at runtime. Because `getClient` runs from the constructor (line 57), every Salesforce service instantiation fails. Add `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma";`.

findings.title: Salesforce now refreshes the token on every client construction, bypasses refreshOAuthTokens, and still uses the old access token
findings.body: Lines 75-99 add an unconditional POST to login.salesforce.com every time the service is constructed. There is no expiry check, and it does not go through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so credential sharing is ignored for Salesforce even though `parseRefreshTokenResponse` is called. A non-OK status throws, and so does a failed parse. The new tokens are saved to the DB, but the `jsforce.Connection` at lines 101-108 is still built from `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.refresh_token`, which are the old values. The refresh therefore adds a network round trip on each booking and does not change the token the connection uses. Wrap the fetch in `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "salesforce", credential.userId)`. Refresh only when the token is expired, or let jsforce refresh through its own `refreshToken` and `refreshFn`. Use `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` for the connection. The zod schema also requires `signature`, `scope` and `id`, which Salesforce refresh responses don't always include.

findings.title: credential.id is passed where a user id is expected
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` receives the credential's row id, but the parameter is the cal.com `userId`. The sync endpoint is sent `calcomUserId=<credential id>` (see `refreshOAuthTokens.ts:11`) and returns tokens for the wrong user. Or it finds no user. Every other call site passes `credential.userId`. Pass `credential.userId`, which means `refreshAccessToken` needs the userId passed in from `biginAuth`.

findings.title: Sync branch returns a raw fetch Response, but most callers expect their SDK/axios result
findings.body:
In sync mode the helper returns the `fetch` Response (line 15). It never checks `response.ok` or parses JSON. Callers written against other shapes break:
- Google (`googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:94`) reads `res?.data`, which is undefined on a Response, so `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The catch at line 103 swallows it, so the token is never refreshed and the failure is silent.
- Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin read `.data.error` and `.data.expires_in`.
- HubSpot reads `.expiresIn` and `.accessToken` on a Response (`hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:192`).

Only the callers that run `handleErrorsJson`, `handleZoomResponse` etc. get a body. Normalise the sync response inside the helper, for example by returning parsed JSON in the shape of the direct call. Or have each caller adapt the sync response. The request also has no `Content-Type` or auth header and no timeout, so a hung endpoint blocks every refresh.

findings.title: Unvalidated body parse and decrypt/JSON.parse failures surface as unhandled 500s
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` (line 31), `symmetricDecrypt` (line 58) and `JSON.parse` (line 57) all throw on bad input: a malformed body, a wrong key or a corrupt ciphertext. There is no try/catch, so the caller gets a generic 500 and the real cause is not logged. Use `safeParse` and return 400. Wrap decrypt and parse and return 400 with a message. Also check that the decrypted `keys` is a non-null object before writing it to `credential.key`. Today any JSON value, such as a string or `null`, would be persisted and break later parsing in each app's service.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with `!==` and no method check
findings.body: The secret comparison is not constant-time, so use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. The handler also accepts any HTTP method. It writes credentials for any app slug found in `appStoreMetadata`, including apps that don't use OAuth. Restrict it to POST. Consider limiting the allowed slugs to the apps that call `refreshOAuthTokens`.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string-or-undefined, not a boolean
findings.body: The `&&` of two env strings yields `string | undefined`: the encryption key's value when both are set. The constant is not used as a plain flag in a single place: `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` also carries the key string through expressions. Wrap it in `Boolean(...)`, or `!!`, so the secret never flows through a value that could be logged or serialised. Also, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` and `refreshOAuthTokens` enable sync on a different condition from the webhook. The webhook needs only the two secrets, while the refresh path also needs `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. That is fine, but document it in `.env.example`.

findings.title: Which slug does the sync endpoint expect for Teams?
findings.body: The appSlug for office365video is `"msteams"`, which matches `office365video/config.json`. The Office365 calendar passes `"office365-calendar"`, Google passes `"google-calendar"`, and Zoom passes `"zoomvideo"`. Please confirm these match the real app slugs, because the webhook looks the slug up in `appStoreMetadata` and returns 404 otherwise. Several (`google-calendar`, `office365-calendar`) could not be confirmed in this review.

findings.title: Credential-sync response is a fetch Response, but the code reads it as an axios response
findings.body: With credential sync on (`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED`, `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` set, and `credential.userId` set), `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` (packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8-15). The code then reads `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` (line 217). A `Response` has no `.data`, so this throws a TypeError. The surrounding `catch` at line 238 only logs it. `this.accessToken` stays `""`, and `createZohoEvent`, `contactSearch` and the other calls send `Zoho-oauthtoken ` with an empty token. Nothing reaches the user: those calls also swallow errors. Zoho CRM events are silently never created or updated whenever sync is on. Parse the sync response (`await response.json()`) and validate it, for example with `parseRefreshTokenResponse` as googlecalendar and office365calendar do. Then store only the fields the sync endpoint returns.

findings.title: Lark refresh breaks under credential sync: response is parsed as Lark's `{code,msg,data}` envelope
findings.body: When sync is enabled, `resp` (line 67) is the sync endpoint's reply. Its comment says it should contain only the access token and expiry date. `handleLarkError` (packages/app-store/larkcalendar/common.ts:13-22) throws unless `data.code === 0`. It then reads `data.data.refresh_token`, `data.data.refresh_expires_in` and `data.data.expires_in` (lines 86-95). A sync response has no `code` or `data` wrapper, so the refresh throws every time. Even if it passed, the code would write `refresh_token: undefined` and NaN expiry values into the credential. Every Lark call that needs a refreshed token fails, and the error is logged and rethrown. In addition, `getAppAccessToken()` (line 66) still makes a Lark API call, and the result is unused in sync mode. Lark is the only refresh call site in this part's calendar services that does not go through `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. It needs a sync-aware branch for the response shape, or it should be left out of `refreshOAuthTokens`.

findings.title: Webex refresh response is validated against the strict native schema, so credential sync always fails
findings.body: With sync on, `response` comes from the sync endpoint and holds only an access token and expiry. Line 88 validates it with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema`. That schema requires `scope` (a literal), `token_type`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in` (lines 49-56). The parse fails and the code rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Webex meeting creation is therefore broken for synced credentials once the access token expires. Zoom, in the same PR, avoids this by calling `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, schema)` (zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:104). Webex has the same pattern but does not use it. Use `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, and keep the stored `refresh_token` and `expiry_date` handling consistent with Zoom.

findings.title: Sync response is written wholesale into the credential key, and expiry is overwritten to "now"
findings.body: With sync on, `responseBody` is the sync endpoint's reply (access token and expiry only). Line 84 overwrites `expiry_date` with `Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000`. If the endpoint returns an expiry under any other name, `expires_in` is undefined and `expiry_date` becomes now. The whole `responseBody` is then saved as `key` (lines 87-95), which replaces the stored credential. `refresh_token`, `scope` and `token_type` are lost. Because `isExpired` is `expiryDate < now` (line 56), the next `getToken` refreshes again, so every Teams call hits the sync endpoint. Compare office365calendar, which runs `parseRefreshTokenResponse` and merges into the existing key (`{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`, office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:263-264). Do the same here: validate with `parseRefreshTokenResponse` and merge into the existing key instead of replacing it.

findings.title: Sync endpoint failures are not distinguished from token errors
findings.body: In sync mode, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` Response without checking `ok`. For a non-2xx reply, `handleErrorsJson` throws `Error(response.statusText)` (packages/lib/errors.ts:24-26), and that message gives no hint that the sync endpoint was the source. For a 2xx reply with an unexpected body, the error at line 81 reads "Error contacting MS Teams", which is also misleading. Consider checking `response.ok` inside `refreshOAuthTokens`, or logging the sync endpoint's status there. This applies to every caller of `refreshOAuthTokens`, not only this file.

contracts.action: Refresh OAuth tokens via external sync endpoint when credential sharing is enabled
contracts.equivalent_path: Direct provider refresh in each app's CalendarService/VideoApiAdapter (the refreshFunction branch, lines 16-19)
contracts.before_after: Before: each app called its provider and parsed the provider's result. After: in sync mode a bare fetch Response is returned to callers written for axios/SDK/fetch shapes; the direct branch is unchanged.
contracts.visible_effect: With sharing enabled, Google, HubSpot and Zoho refreshes fail or are swallowed, so calendars or CRM integrations stop working once tokens expire.
contracts.failure_mode: Network rejection or non-2xx from the endpoint is not handled in the helper; no timeout; Response has no .data.

contracts.visible_effect: Credentials for a user and app are created or replaced without user interaction.
contracts.failure_mode: Bad body, wrong key or bad ciphertext throws and gives an unhandled 500; non-object decrypted JSON is stored as the credential key.

contracts.action: Salesforce service now refreshes tokens on construction
contracts.equivalent_path: Other app services refresh only when token is expired, through refreshOAuthTokens
contracts.before_after: Before: Connection built from stored credential only. After: a network refresh on every instantiation, then a Connection still built from the old tokens.
contracts.visible_effect: Extra latency per booking; fails outright because prisma is not imported.
contracts.failure_mode: Non-OK status throws HttpError 400 from the constructor's promise; ReferenceError for prisma.

contracts.action: Zoho CRM token refresh now goes through refreshOAuthTokens (credential-sync branch)
contracts.equivalent_path: googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:86-97 and office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:246-264 call refreshOAuthTokens, then parse the result with parseRefreshTokenResponse.
contracts.before_after: Before: axios POST result was read as `.data`. After: in sync mode the result is a fetch Response, and `.data.error` is read directly with no parsing.
contracts.visible_effect: Zoho CRM events are silently not created or updated when credential sync is on.
contracts.failure_mode: TypeError on `.data.error` is caught at line 238 and only logged. `accessToken` stays empty and later API calls swallow their own errors.

contracts.equivalent_path: Same refresh path before the PR: direct fetch followed by handleLarkError.
contracts.before_after: Before: Lark's own `{code,msg,data}` response was parsed. After: in sync mode, the sync endpoint's response is passed to the same Lark-specific parser.
contracts.visible_effect: Lark calendar calls fail once the access token expires, if sync is enabled.
contracts.failure_mode: handleLarkError throws the response body as an error. This is logged and rethrown from refreshAccessToken, and the fetcher wraps it as "get access token error".

contracts.action: Webex and Office365 video refresh routed through refreshOAuthTokens
contracts.before_after: Webex still validates with the strict native schema, and Office365 video stores the raw response. Zoom uses the relaxed sync-aware parser.
contracts.visible_effect: Webex meeting creation fails and Teams credentials are damaged when sync is on.
contracts.failure_mode: Webex rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Office365 video overwrites the key and forces a refresh on every call.

contracts.action: Import path moves for encodeOAuthState, decodeOAuthState and createOAuthAppCredential in api/add.ts and api/callback.ts
contracts.equivalent_path: The old paths under _utils/ are no longer referenced anywhere.
contracts.before_after: Same functions, new path under _utils/oauth/. No behavioural change.
contracts.failure_mode: A stale import would fail at build time. A repo-wide search for the old paths found no matches.

summary:
**Batch 1 of 1.** The core of this PR is broken in several ways. Four findings are blockers:
- Google credential corruption: the Google service stores the safeParse result object, `{ success, data }`, as the credential key.
- Broken schema: the computed key `[z.string().toString()]` is the literal string "[object Object]", so the sync-mode schema can never match a real response.
- Missing import: the Salesforce service calls `prisma` without importing it.
- Wrong id: the Zoho Bigin refresh passes the credential id where a user id is expected.

Beyond those:
- In sync mode, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw Response that Google, HubSpot and the Zoho services cannot read.
- The webhook handler has unhandled 500s and no body validation.
- Salesforce now refreshes on every instantiation and then uses the old token.

**Batch 1 of 1, retry.** The import path moves in the add.ts and callback.ts files are mechanical and consistent. A search of the repo found no stale references to the old paths. The refresh-token call sites in Lark, Webex, Office365 video and Zoho CRM do not handle the credential-sync response correctly. The sync branch of `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch Response, and each of those four parses it with its own native schema or axios shape. The result is four fixes: Zoho CRM fails silently, Lark and Webex reject the sync response, and Office365 video overwrites the stored credential key. Zoom, Google Calendar and Office365 Calendar use `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, which these four skip.
